clue.text: Lucre could be corrupting influence

indicators.note: could be suggests the word Lucre might turn into something else once its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Money, filthy lucre, may be the thing that corrupts people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could be' signals an anagram of LUCRE, which gives ULCER.
explanation.definitionFit: Figuratively an ulcer is a festering, corroding presence that eats away at something from within.

clue.text: National treasure once — Robert in foreign town is 20 21

indicators.note: foreign suggests the words once, Robert and in are made strange, scrambled into a new order

parts.note: T is a standard abbreviation for town, as on maps

explanation.surface: A much-loved entertainer from the past, born Robert, living in a town abroad, reaches a milestone age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foreign' turns ONCE ROBERT IN into RONNIE CORBE, then T is added. Ronnie Corbett was a British comedian, one of The Two Ronnies; '20 21' points to EIGHTY TODAY, his age when the puzzle appeared.
explanation.definitionFit: The comedian was a beloved British entertainer, widely called a national treasure by the press and public.

clue.text: See 2
Climbing snake caught escaping to right of trees

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means the letters go upwards, so the trimmed snake is read in reverse
escaping says the letter for caught gets away, leaving the snake's name

parts.note: a cobra is a venomous snake
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
right as in 'a right mess' means real, genuine

explanation.surface: A snake slips up a tree and away to the right before anyone can catch it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climbing' suits a down clue: the trimmed snake is read upwards. 'Right' gives REAL as in 'a right mess', and 'to' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Arboreal describes things that live in or relate to trees, such as tree-dwelling animals.

clue.text: Cummings wears tight leggings — not good, they're revealing

indicators.note: wears means the poet's initials are put on inside the rearranged leggings, like clothing round a body
tight in the sense of drunk signals that the leggings letters reel into a new order
not good says one letter for good is left out of the leggings

parts.note: the American poet E. E. Cummings, known by his initials

explanation.surface: A man named Cummings is wearing skintight leggings, and it is not a pretty sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tight' means drunk here, an anagram signal, not a description of the leggings; 'wears' puts the poet's initials inside the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Negligees are flimsy, sheer nightgowns, which show a lot of the wearer.

clue.text: Russian mole government's revealed

indicators.note: revealed says the name sits in plain sight inside the run of letters of mole government's

explanation.surface: A spy embedded in the government has been exposed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revealed' shows the name inside mOLE Government's. 'Mole' and 'revealed' make it look like a spy story.
explanation.definitionFit: Oleg is a common Russian man's name, so it stands for a Russian person.

clue.text: Bird or fish part? Check!

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
a fin is part of a fish
CH is the chess abbreviation for check

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether something is a bird or a bit of fish, with a call to verify it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like a link word between bird and fish, but it is the heraldry term for the metal. 'Check' gives the chess notation.
explanation.definitionFit: The goldfinch is a small songbird with bright yellow wing bars.

clue.text: "Hard to love" is lingering impression

indicators.note: to says the word for hard is attached onto the end of the letter for love

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scoring, written O
dour means hard, stern

explanation.surface: Someone says they are difficult to love, which has left a lasting mark on them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' means DOUR is put after O. O is love because love means a score of nil in tennis.
explanation.definitionFit: A smell can hang in the air after its source has gone, so it is a sensory trace that stays.

clue.text: Was Sorry about to be proclaimed offensive?

indicators.note: to be proclaimed means the word for offensive is announced, so we want what it sounds like when spoken

parts.note: rude means offensive, impolite

explanation.surface: Someone regretted something they said aloud that others found offensive.
explanation.walkthrough: RUDE (offensive) said out loud sounds like RUED.
explanation.definitionFit: To rue something is to regret it, so the past tense means felt remorse over.

clue.text: Impulsive son let out a little cheer

indicators.note: let out says the letter for son is released from the word for impulsive

parts.note: rash means impulsive, hasty
S is the standard abbreviation for son, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: A headstrong boy is freed and gives a small whoop.
explanation.walkthrough: RASH loses its S (son, 'let out'), leaving RAH.
explanation.definitionFit: Rah is a short exclamation of encouragement, a brief shout of support.

clue.text: Attacked criminal with a bit of lead inside

indicators.note: inside says the small piece of lead goes within the word for criminal

parts.note: a felon is a criminal

indicators.note: a bit of picks just the opening letter of lead

explanation.surface: A villain was set upon, and has a bullet lodged in him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit of' takes L from 'lead', and 'inside' puts it in FELON to give FEL-L-ON. 'Lead' makes you think of a bullet.
explanation.definitionFit: To fall on someone is to set upon or assault them suddenly.

clue.text: Army general comes to harm in cemetery

parts.note: William Booth founded the Salvation Army and was its first General
ill as a noun means harm, as in 'wish no ill'

explanation.surface: A military commander ends up getting hurt, and lands in the graveyard.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Army' is the Salvation Army, whose leader is called its General; William Booth was the first. 'Comes to' just joins BOOTH and ILL.
explanation.definitionFit: Boot Hill is the name given to Wild West graveyards where gunfighters were buried with their boots on.

clue.text: Swift novel left (featuring a little Endian)

indicators.note: featuring says the small part of Endian appears within the reworked letters of left
novel as an adjective means new, so the word left is given a new arrangement
a little takes only the opening letter of Endian

explanation.surface: Jonathan Swift's novel Gulliver's Travels features Big-Endians and Little-Endians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swift' and 'novel' suggest Gulliver's Travels, whose Lilliputians fight over which end to crack an egg. 'Novel' rearranges LEFT, and 'featuring' puts E (from 'a little Endian') inside to give FLEET.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleet means fast, quick on one's feet.

clue.text: Issue as engineers return

indicators.note: return says the two pieces are brought back, read from right to left

parts.note: eg, for example, can stand for as in 'such as'
REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British Army corps

explanation.surface: A question about publishing a magazine edition when the engineers come back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' reverses EG + REME to give EMERGE. REME is a British Army corps of engineers.
explanation.definitionFit: To issue is to come out or flow forth, as people come out of a building.

clue.text: Right away, refrains from employing Express writers

indicators.note: employing says the cut-down word takes on the word for express inside it
away says the letter for right is taken out of the word for refrains from

parts.note: to resist doing something is to refrain from it
to say something is to express it

explanation.surface: Columnists at the Express newspaper turn down jobs one after another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Express' looks like the newspaper's name but is the verb to say. 'Right away' drops R, and 'employing' takes the verb inside what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Essayists write essays, short prose pieces, so they are authors of a kind.

clue.text: Head's brief: to kill American staff officer

indicators.note: brief means cut short, so the word for head loses its final letter

parts.note: poll is an old word for the head, as in poll tax
ice is American slang for kill
to staff a post is to man it

explanation.surface: A headteacher's legal brief describes killing an American staff member.
explanation.walkthrough: POLL (head) cut short ('brief') gives POL. ICE is US slang for kill, and MAN means to staff. 'Brief' makes you think of a lawyer's brief.
explanation.definitionFit: A policeman is an officer of the law, often just called an officer.

clue.text: Ex-footballer's sons use ground

indicators.note: ground means crushed and broken up, so the letters of sons use are reduced and reformed

explanation.surface: A retired footballer's children play at his old stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like a football ground but means crushed: it rearranges SONS USE. Graeme Souness is a former Scotland and Liverpool footballer. The 's means 'is', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Graeme Souness is a retired Scottish footballer, so the clue names him by his former career.

clue.text: Declare one run ahead initially after leg bye

indicators.note: after says the one, run and initial pieces come behind the word for leg

parts.note: to declare is to say
on is the leg side in cricket
a means one
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

indicators.note: initially takes just the opening letter of ahead

explanation.surface: A cricket captain declares as his side goes a run ahead, after the umpire signals a leg bye.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket terms mislead: 'leg' gives ON (the leg side), R is run. 'After' puts A, R and A behind ON. SAYONARA is Japanese for goodbye.
explanation.definitionFit: Sayonara is the Japanese word for farewell, used in English as a jokey goodbye.

clue.text: Goes on about large emblem of the 2 2s

indicators.note: about says the word for goes on is placed round the letter for large

parts.note: to gas is to talk on and on, so gasses means goes on
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A chatterbox goes on about an outsized badge.
explanation.walkthrough: '2 2s' means 'Two' plus 2-down's first word: The Two Ronnies, whose title sequence featured a pair of spectacles. 'About' puts L inside GASSES.
explanation.definitionFit: The comedy show's logo was a pair of spectacles, and both stars wore them.

clue.text: Stumped — poor fellow with suspended sentence

parts.note: ST is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for stumped

indicators.note: suspended means the letter for with is put on hold and dropped from the word for poor fellow

parts.note: a wretch is a poor unfortunate person

explanation.surface: A baffled unfortunate man is let off with a suspended sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspended sentence' looks like a single legal term. In fact 'with suspended' drops W from WRETCH, and 'sentence' alone is the definition, since a stretch is a prison term.
explanation.definitionFit: Stretch is slang for a term in prison.

clue.text: Scores shouted at constituents

indicators.note: shouted means the letters are spoken aloud, giving a sound we then write as a word

parts.note: the parts that make up the word at are the letters A and T

explanation.surface: Football results are being yelled at the team's supporters.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of 'at', said one by one (A, T), sound like EIGHTY. 'Constituents' looks like voters but means component letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A score is twenty, so four scores make up that number.

clue.text: Now crawler's backing Democrat

indicators.note: backing says the letter for Democrat is pushed back to a later spot in the word for crawler

parts.note: a toady is a crawler, a sycophant; the 's means 'is' and gives no letter
D is the US abbreviation for Democrat

explanation.surface: A sycophant is currently supporting a Democratic politician.
explanation.walkthrough: In TOADY the D moves back one place ('backing') to give TODAY. 'Backing' looks like political support.
explanation.definitionFit: Today, in the sense of nowadays, means at the present time.

clue.text: Silk with obscure prosecutor

parts.note: DA is a District Attorney, the American public prosecutor
to mask something is to obscure it

explanation.surface: A barrister, a silk, works alongside a shadowy prosecutor.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'silk' is a senior British barrister (a King's Counsel), so the surface reads as a courtroom. 'With' only joins the two pieces; the clue gives them in reverse order.
explanation.definitionFit: Damask is a rich patterned fabric, originally of silk.

clue.text: Raised line dividing top and bottom

indicators.note: in a down clue raised means the letters are lifted to read upwards
dividing says the letter for line splits the word for top

parts.note: a roof is the top of a building

explanation.surface: A raised line separates the upper and lower parts of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dividing' puts L inside ROOF to give ROOLF, and 'Raised' reverses it to FLOOR. 'Top and bottom' look like a pair, but 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The floor is the lowest surface of a room, the base underfoot.

clue.text: Neil angry at money Papa spent — it's not strictly affordable

indicators.note: angry suggests the name Neil is stirred up and thrown into disorder
spent means used up, so the letter for Papa is gone from the money

parts.note: pence is British money
P is Papa in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Neil is cross that his father has wasted money: they can't afford to be soft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Angry' rearranges NEIL into LENI. PENCE without P (Papa, 'spent') gives ENCE. Leniency is something people grant or 'afford' to others, not strictly.
explanation.definitionFit: Lenience is mercy shown or granted without strictness, such as a light punishment.

clue.text: One about to show anger

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: Someone is on the verge of losing their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To show' is a link between the wordplay and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ire is wrath, a literary word for rage.

clue.text: Girl's dumping a spritely fellow — me!

indicators.note: dumping says the girl's name drops the letter a, as a partner is dropped

parts.note: Amy is a girl's name, and the 's gives a letter S here
an elf is a sprite, a small mischievous being

explanation.surface: A girl ditches her lively boyfriend, who cries 'what about me?'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dumping a' drops that letter from the girl's name, keeping the S of the possessive. 'Spritely' looks like 'sprightly' (lively) but means sprite-like.
explanation.definitionFit: Myself is the emphatic or reflexive form of the first person, standing for the speaker.

clue.text: Broad's senseless over to Aussie tail-ender

indicators.note: over says the word for senseless is turned round, read backwards

parts.note: mad means senseless, crazy

indicators.note: tail-ender takes the final letter of Aussie, its tail

explanation.surface: A woman is crazy about an Australian cricketer who bats last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' reverses MAD to DAM, and 'tail-ender' gives E, the last letter of 'Aussie'. A tail-ender is also a low-order cricket batsman. 'Broad' is slang for a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are words for a woman: broad as American slang, dame as a dated colloquialism.

clue.text: Scare off groups of people

indicators.note: off suggests the word scare has gone wrong, its letters disordered

explanation.surface: An order to frighten some people away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off' signals an anagram of SCARE. 'Scare off' looks like a single phrasal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Races are populations sharing ancestry, so they are human groupings.

clue.text: Go away, much disturbed

indicators.note: much here means most of but not all, so the word for disturbed loses its last letter

parts.note: shook means shaken up, disturbed

explanation.surface: Someone, badly upset, tells another to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Much' means most of SHOOK, so it drops the final K to give SHOO.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoo is an exclamation used to chase off an animal or person.
